From around the middle of the 1700s, fleets of boats sailed each year from Makassar in South Sulawesi to the coast of northern Australia to gather trepang, or sea cucumber. They came with the northwest monsoon in December and left with the southeast winds a few months later.

The crews collected sea cucumbers in the shallows, boiled and dried them in camps on the shore, and sold them in Makassar to Chinese merchants, who shipped them to China of the Qing era, where they were prized in cooking and medicine. They worked first in the Kimberley and later in Arnhem Land.

On the coast they traded with Aboriginal people, especially the Yolŋu, giving cloth, tobacco, metal knives and dugout canoes. Some Yolŋu sailed back to Makassar. Makassan words entered Yolŋu languages, and the visits appear in their art and ceremonies. In 1803 the explorer Matthew Flinders met a Makassan fleet. The South Australian government, which then ran the Northern Territory, taxed the trade and ended it in 1906 and 1907. It is the best recorded early foreign trade of Aboriginal Australia.
